title: Vivienne Returned
warm:
At 6:12 on a Wednesday morning in late October, Rhea Quinn picked up her pen and made a mark on the slate under *Greer, V.* for the first time in eleven months.

[player_name] heard about it later from Rhea herself, who told the story the way she told everything, quietly and with her hands folded on the desk: the revolving door turning in the gray dawn, the doorman going pale, and a woman in a camel coat crossing the lobby as if she had simply been out for a very long walk. Thinner than before. Hair shorter. No luggage. She had stopped at the desk, looked Rhea straight in the eye, and said, "Good morning, Rhea. I believe I'm expected to sign in."

Rhea had handed her the pen. Vivienne Greer had signed. Then she had asked to use the house phone, and she had called Detective Imani Brooks.

By noon it was everywhere. By evening, Crownspire's lobby was full of news vans, and [player_name] sat on the floor of her own apartment with her back against the door, listening to the building hum with a sound she had never heard it make before. Not hush. Not gossip. Something closer to relief, and closer to shame.

Nolan had not come home. He had been out all night, hunting—driving the coast roads after the plane-desk handler who had slipped Brooks's net, answering calls from men [player_name] didn't know, coming back to her at dawn some mornings gray-faced and silent. She had waited across the hall through all of it. She had not known what she was waiting for.

Not this.

The knock came at nine. Not three measured taps. Two, light and brisk, a knock she had never heard.

She knew before she opened the door.

Vivienne Greer stood in the hall in the camel coat, exactly where [player_name] had seen her through the peephole on the night of the fourteenth. Up close she was smaller than she had seemed crossing the lobby all those years. Her face was bare, and tired, and very composed.

"May I come in?" she said. "I think it's time you and I spoke without a door between us."

They sat in [player_name]'s kitchen. [player_name] made tea because she did not know what else to do with her hands. Vivienne held the cup without drinking.

"I'll tell you what I told the detective," she said. "Then I'll tell you what I didn't."

What she had told Brooks: that she had left the marriage on her own. That she had arranged the thinning visits herself, week to month to gone, so that when she vanished it would look like drift instead of flight. That Marcus Pell had given her money—a great deal of it—to go quietly and stay gone, and she had taken it. That the handler had flown her to the coast and she had walked away from the airfield into a life under another name, and she had left her passport and her phone behind precisely so no one could follow. That she had come back because she had read, in a newspaper in a café a very long way from here, that a man was being hunted for her murder, and that her husband's neighbor was being called his accomplice, and she found that she could not let either lie stand.

"I've given the money back," she said. "Every cent. Marcus was not pleased."

"And what didn't you tell her?"

Vivienne looked at her for a long time. "That I chose you," she said. "Not by name. I didn't know your name. But I knew there was someone across the hall. I saw the way his door stayed open. I thought: good. Someone will be there. He's a hard man to leave alone, and I needed to leave him."

[player_name]'s throat was tight. "You left me holding your absence."

"Yes. I'm sorry for that. Truly." Vivienne set down the cup. "I didn't expect you to love him. And I certainly didn't expect him to let you."

There was no anger in it. Only a strange, tired recognition, one woman to another, across a kitchen table in a glass tower where both of them had once been kept.

"What happens now?" [player_name] asked.

"Now I sign papers. Marcus draws up something ruinously fair. I take a small place on the sixth floor for a while, because I find I don't want to run anymore, and I'd like to be able to buy my own coffee in the lobby without it being a scandal." A faint, dry smile. "And I take my perfume out of that bathroom. I should have done it years ago."

She rose. At the door she paused and looked back.

"He's in the hall," she said. "He's been standing there for ten minutes, trying to decide whether he's allowed to knock. I'd put him out of his misery."

Then she was gone, her brisk footsteps fading toward the elevator, and the chime sounded, and the car took her down.

[player_name] stood very still in her kitchen. Then she walked to her door and opened it.

Nolan was there. Unshaven, still in last night's coat, eyes red-rimmed. He looked like a man who had driven all night toward one ending and arrived at another. For a moment neither of them spoke.

"She's alive," he said. His voice cracked on it.

"She's alive."

"I didn't— I never knew. Pell never told me where. I thought—" He stopped, pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes, and let out a breath that shook his whole frame. "Eleven months I thought I might have paid for something I couldn't live with."

She took his wrists and brought his hands down so she could see his face.

Behind him, across the hall, his door stood open. From inside, faintly, came the sound of Vivienne's housekeeper already clearing the master bath—bottles clinking, a drawer sliding shut, the last of an old perfume leaving the air.

"Come home," Nolan said. Then, catching himself, softer, like a man learning a new language: "Or let me come to yours. Or—I don't care which door. I just don't want a hallway between us anymore."

[player_name] looked at his open door, and at hers, and at the twelve steps of carpet that had held every secret of the last year.

She stepped out into the hall.
hot:
Vivienne Greer came back on a Wednesday at dawn, signed Rhea Quinn's slate for the first time in eleven months, called Detective Imani Brooks from the house phone, and by nine o'clock was sitting at [player_name]'s kitchen table with an untouched cup of tea, telling her everything.

She'd left on her own. She'd thinned the calendar herself, week to month to gone, so her leaving would look like drift. Marcus Pell had paid her a fortune to go quietly, and she'd taken it. The handler had flown her to the coast; she'd walked away from the airfield into another name and left her passport and phone so no one could follow. She'd come back because she read in a café a world away that a man was being hunted for her murder, and that her husband's neighbor was being called his accomplice, and she found she couldn't let it stand. She'd given the money back. Every cent.

"I knew there was someone across the hall," she said at the door. "I thought: good. He's a hard man to leave alone." A dry smile. "I didn't expect you to love him. Or him to let you. He's in the hall, by the way. He's been standing there ten minutes."

Then she was gone, and the elevator chimed, and [player_name] opened her door.

Nolan stood there unshaven in last night's coat, eyes red from driving the coast roads all night hunting a handler who'd slipped Brooks's net. He looked wrecked. He looked like a man who'd braced for one ending and been handed another.

"She's alive," he said, and his voice broke.

"She's alive."

"Eleven months I thought I'd paid for something I couldn't live with."

She pulled him inside by his coat and kissed him.

It wasn't gentle. It was eleven months of dread breaking open all at once—his hands in her hair, her back against the entry wall, his mouth hungry and shaking on hers. She shoved the coat off his shoulders. He dragged her sweater over her head. They didn't make it past the hallway mirror; he lifted her against the wall and she wrapped her legs around him and felt how hard he was through his trousers, and she was already wet, already aching, already past caring about anything but getting him inside her.

"Here," she gasped. "Now."

He fumbled his belt open one-handed, shoved her skirt up, pulled her underwear aside, and pushed into her in one long stroke that made them both cry out. For a moment he just held there, buried deep, forehead against hers, breathing like he'd surfaced from underwater.

"No ghost," he whispered.

"No ghost."

He fucked her against the wall hard and fast and desperate, her shoulder blades knocking the plaster, the mirror rattling on its hook, every thrust punching a sound out of her she didn't bother to muffle. Let the hall hear. Let the whole building hear. There was no secret left to keep. She came first, clenching around him so hard he swore, and he came seconds later, pinning her to the wall, groaning her name into her neck while his hips jerked against hers.

Later—much later—he took her across the hall.

The penthouse was different. She felt it the moment they walked in: the air lighter, emptier. He led her by the hand to the master bath, and the marble counter was bare. The perfume was gone. Vivienne's housekeeper had cleared it that morning; the drawers stood empty, the mirror clean. Just stone and glass and morning light.

Nolan turned on the shower and undressed her slowly under the spray, and this time it was unhurried—his soapy hands sliding over her breasts, her belly, between her thighs, touching her as if for the first time in a room that had never let him. She knelt on the warm wet stone and took him in her mouth, water streaming down her back, and sucked him until his hand braced against the tile and his thighs shook. Then he lifted her up, turned her to face the glass, and slid into her from behind, slow and deep, his arm banded across her chest, his mouth at her ear.

"Stay," he said, moving inside her. "Not across the hall. Not as anything to hide. Just stay."

She reached back and gripped his hip and pulled him deeper, and she came with her palm flat against the fogged glass and his name echoing off bare marble where another woman's perfume had waited for years.

Afterward, wrapped in his robe, she stood in his doorway and looked across at her own door, twelve steps away, still standing open.

Two doors. One hall. No ghost.

Nolan came up behind her and rested his chin on her shoulder. His hands slid inside the robe and settled warm on her bare stomach, and her body answered him instantly, shamelessly, as if it had already decided.

"Which door?" he murmured.

She leaned back into him and didn't answer yet.
